# Frame Inventory

Application for the frame-inventory take-home exercise.

## System Overview

Next.js serves the inventory and import workspace. It sends GraphQL requests through a same-origin route to the BFF, which calls Spring Boot over gRPC. Docker Compose runs these services alongside PostgreSQL, Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Alloy, and the OpenTelemetry Collector. The exercise provides a legacy export in `data/inventory_frame.csv` and describes the inventory features in `INSTRUCTIONS.md`.

Bring the whole stack up with one command.

```bash
docker compose up --build
```

Once PostgreSQL is healthy, the backend applies pending Flyway migrations during startup.

If you have `just` installed, run `just` to list the available recipes.

| Command | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| `just up` | Build and start the whole stack in the foreground. |
| `just down` | Stop the stack and retain its named data volumes. |
| `just compose logs -f backend` | Pass arguments through to Docker Compose. |
| `just migrate` | Run Flyway on its own in a one-off backend container. |

## Subdirectories & System Boundaries

- [Application source](./src/README.md) contains the Spring Boot backend, Apollo Server BFF, and Next.js frontend.
- [Design system](./design-system/README.md) contains the prototype, sample frame data, and visual conventions for the exercise.

## Services

`docker compose up` starts the following services.

| Service               | Host port | Container port | Notes                                                  |
|-----------------------|-----------|----------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| frontend              | 3000      | 3000           | Next.js workspace and same-origin GraphQL route     |
| bff                   | 4000      | 4000           | Apollo Sandbox and the frame inventory GraphQL API     |
| backend               | 8080      | 8080           | Spring Boot, exposes `GET /api/health`                 |
| postgres              | 5432      | 5432           | Spring Boot applies the inventory schema via Flyway    |
| prometheus            | 9091      | 9090           | Scrapes Spring Boot and Apollo metrics every 15 seconds |
| otel-collector        | 9464      | 9464           | Scrapes Spring Boot metrics for local inspection       |
| grafana               | 3001      | 3000           | Queries provisioned Prometheus and Loki data            |

### Credentials

| Service               | User       | Password       | Database         |
|-----------------------|------------|----------------|------------------|
| postgres              | `app`      | `app`          | `frames`         |
| grafana               | `admin`    | `admin`         | n/a              |

## Global Invariants

- The Next.js rewrite preserves the `/api/` path and uses `BACKEND_URL` as its destination origin. Compose sets it to `http://backend:8080`. `[src/frontend/next.config.ts:rewrites]` `[docker-compose.yml:services.frontend.environment.BACKEND_URL]`
- The Next.js `/api/graphql` route proxies GraphQL to `BFF_URL`. Compose sets it to `http://bff:4000`.

## Global Side Effects

- Opening the frontend loads the first page of frames. Starting an import uploads the file directly to S3 using the signed URL returned by the BFF.
- Docker Compose publishes service ports and creates named volumes for PostgreSQL, Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, and Alloy. `[docker-compose.yml:services]` `[docker-compose.yml:volumes]`

## System Verification

- From `src/backend`, run `./gradlew test`.
- From `src/frontend`, run `npm run lint` after installing dependencies.

### Git hooks

Install [pre-commit](https://pre-commit.com/#installation), then run `pre-commit install`
from the repository root to install both Git hooks. The `pre-commit` hook checks
YAML, JSON, and merge conflict markers, and runs ESLint when staged changes touch
`src/frontend/`. Install the frontend dependencies with `npm ci --prefix src/frontend`
before committing frontend changes.

The `commit-msg` hook uses Commitlint to enforce the Conventional Commits format
documented in [AGENTS.md](./AGENTS.md). Commitlint requires Node.js 22.12 or newer.

Run `pre-commit run --all-files` to check the whole repository.

### Smoke test

Once the stack is up, check the service entry points.

- Open <http://localhost:3000> to view the frame list. See the [frontend setup](./src/frontend/README.md) to enable local imports.
- Hit the backend directly: <http://localhost:8080/api/health>.
- Open [Apollo Sandbox](http://127.0.0.1:4000) and run the [frame list query](./src/bff/README.md).

### Backend metrics

- Open [Prometheus Targets](http://127.0.0.1:9091/targets) and wait for the
  `frame-inventory-backend` target to show **UP**. It scrapes
  `http://backend:8080/actuator/prometheus` on the Compose network.
- Open [Grafana](http://127.0.0.1:3001), sign in with the initial credentials
  above, and run `up{job="frame-inventory-backend"}` in **Explore** using the
  default Prometheus data source. A value of `1` confirms the backend is being scraped.
- Open [Frame Inventory Backend](http://127.0.0.1:3001/d/frame-inventory-backend/frame-inventory-backend)
  for HTTP and gRPC request rate, errors, p50, p95, and p99 latency, and resource saturation.
  Generate API traffic and allow at least two Prometheus scrapes for request graphs
  to populate.
- The **Frame inventory activity** section shows committed creates, updates, and
  soft deletes, plus successful gRPC reads and version conflicts. The totals cover
  the dashboard time range. Rejected or rolled-back writes and repeated deletes
  that change no data are excluded from the totals.

Prometheus and Grafana listen on localhost. Their named volumes keep metrics
and Grafana settings across restarts.

### DELTA import dashboard

For the host-based [local import setup](src/backend/README.md#local-import-operator),
start Spring Boot with the dispatcher and worker enabled. Set
`MANAGEMENT_ENDPOINTS_WEB_EXPOSURE_INCLUDE=health,info,prometheus` and keep HTTP
port 8080 reachable from Docker. On Docker Desktop, scrape that host backend
with the local import Compose override.

```sh
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f monitoring/compose.local-import.yml \
  up -d --no-deps prometheus grafana
```

Open [Frame Inventory Imports](http://127.0.0.1:3001/d/frame-inventory-imports/frame-inventory-imports)
to see the oldest pending and running jobs, terminal dispatch failures in the
last hour, and mean and p95 apply duration. The age uses dispatch confirmation
when available and job creation otherwise. Apply duration covers each activity
attempt, including retries. Use the import job ID to find its
`csv-import-<jobId>` workflow when investigating a specific job.

To return to scraping the containerized backend and BFF, run
`docker compose up -d prometheus grafana` with the standard Compose configuration.

### BFF metrics

Run `docker compose up -d --build bff prometheus grafana`. If Prometheus was
already running, reload its scrape configuration with
`docker compose restart prometheus`. Confirm that `frame-inventory-bff` is
**UP** in [Prometheus Targets](http://127.0.0.1:9091/targets). Prometheus scrapes
`http://bff:9465/metrics` on the Compose network.

Open [Frame Inventory BFF](http://127.0.0.1:3001/d/frame-inventory-bff/frame-inventory-bff)
for GraphQL request rate, error percentage, p50/p95/p99 latency, in-flight
requests, and event loop utilization. The **Slowest queries and mutations (p95)**
panel ranks top-level fields such as `frames` and `updateFrame` by resolver
latency over the selected time range. Run the [frame list query](./src/bff/README.md)
several times across at least two scrapes. Run `{ frames(page: -1) { page } }`
to generate a GraphQL error. The dashboard counts GraphQL errors even when
Apollo responds with HTTP 200.

### Backend and BFF logs

Run `docker compose up -d --build bff grafana`. Alloy reads the backend and
BFF containers’ stdout and stderr through the Docker socket and sends them
to Loki. Loki stores logs in the `loki-data` volume with seven-day retention.
For a failed GraphQL request, take the `X-Correlation-Id` response header
and search both services with
`{service_name=~"backend|bff"} | json | correlationId="your-id"`.
For a production deployment, configure log storage, retention, and access
controls for that environment.

Open [Grafana Explore](http://127.0.0.1:3001/explore), select **Loki**,
and switch to **Code** mode to run either LogQL query.

- Backend — `{service_name="backend"}`
- BFF — `{service_name="bff"}`

### OpenTelemetry Collector

Run `docker compose up -d --build otel-collector` to start the Collector and its
dependencies. The Collector scrapes `http://backend:8080/actuator/prometheus`
every 15 seconds and exposes the latest samples on localhost. Once the backend
is ready and the first scrape completes, check for a JVM metric from Spring Boot.

```bash
curl --fail --silent --show-error http://127.0.0.1:9464/metrics | rg '^jvm_memory_used_bytes\{'
```

### Backend

Start PostgreSQL before running the backend locally. Spring Boot applies the
Flyway migrations on startup.

```bash
docker compose up -d --wait postgres
cd src/backend
./gradlew bootRun
```

### Frontend

```bash
cd src/frontend
npm install
npm run dev
```

## Inventory import development services

See [inventory import infrastructure](infra/inventory-import/README.md) for the
opt-in S3/SQS emulator and Temporal profile, Terraform, and smoke test.

## Sentry error reporting

Set `SENTRY_DSN` to the DSN of the backend's Sentry project and set
`SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT` to the environment name, such as `staging`. The environment
defaults to `local`. An empty or unset DSN disables error reporting.

Export the variables before running `./gradlew bootRun` from `src/backend`.
For Docker Compose, export the same variables or set them in an untracked
`.env` file at the repository root, then run `docker compose up --build -d backend`
to rebuild and apply the settings.

To verify reporting, use a non-production Sentry project or environment. In a
local checkout, temporarily make a controller handler throw an
`IllegalStateException` with a unique test message and call that route. Confirm
the event appears in Sentry with the expected stack trace and environment tag,
then link the event on the issue. Remove the temporary exception and confirm
`curl --fail http://localhost:8080/api/health` succeeds with the DSN configured
and again after restarting the backend with the DSN unset.

### Local import operator

The import RPC service attaches `LocalImportIdentity` as a service-scoped
interceptor. Existing frame RPCs do not use it. Enable Spring's `local-import`
profile only for host-local development and set `INVENTORY_IMPORT_LOCAL_TOKEN`
to a randomly generated 64-character lowercase hex value. Keep the credential
out of source control and logs. The RPC accepts the credential as
`authorization: Bearer <token>` only from a loopback peer and sets the fixed
`local-import-operator` identity. The interceptor checks the actual transport
peer. The Spring gRPC server can still listen on all interfaces.

The import BFF must run on the same host, accept the credential only for import
operations, and forward it alongside the existing correlation metadata. Do not
derive operator identity from a browser-supplied ID or treat ordinary frame RPC
authentication as an import credential. The single local operator can create
DELTA jobs and request force overwrite. The service rejects FULL_SNAPSHOT until the snapshot safety checks ship. Persist the verified
operator as job owner and check ownership before returning status or row
diagnostics. Production imports remain disabled until an operator identity
provider and permission policy are configured.


### Local import RPCs

Start PostgreSQL and the `aws` Compose service. Run Spring Boot on the host
with the `local-import` profile and configure these additional variables:

| Variable | Local value |
| --- | --- |
| `INVENTORY_IMPORT_BUCKET` | `frame-inventory-import-local` |
| `INVENTORY_IMPORT_REGION` | `us-east-1` |
| `INVENTORY_IMPORT_SIGNING_ENDPOINT` | `http://127.0.0.1:4566` |
| `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` | `test` |
| `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` | `test` |

`InventoryImport.CreateImportJob` creates a DELTA job and returns a PUT URL
valid for 15 minutes. Send every returned header unchanged, including
`If-None-Match: *` and the CSV content type. The caller can read the durable
summary with `GetImportJob` and the diagnostics with `ListImportRowErrors`.
Diagnostics are ordered by data row number and error code. Pages are zero-based
and default to 25 items.

`AWAITING_UPLOAD` becomes `PENDING` when dispatch binds the first accepted
object version. Dispatch must validate the event and pass the upload time and
the decoded key to the repository. A timely upload may arrive for another
15 minutes after URL expiry. The job becomes `EXPIRED` if it still has no
object at the dispatch deadline. Subsequent dispatch and worker work will move
`PENDING` to `RUNNING` and then to a terminal result. An unrecoverable dispatch
failure can move `PENDING` directly to `FAILED`. Re-delivery of the bound
version preserves its identity and status. A different version is rejected.

Final job summaries and the frame-version reference are durable. Row

# AGENTS.md - Java Spring Boot & gRPC Development Guidelines

Behavioral and architectural guidelines to reduce common LLM coding mistakes while strictly enforcing **SOLID principles**, Spring Boot + gRPC best practices, and clean code standards.

**Tradeoff:** These guidelines bias toward caution over speed. For trivial tasks, use judgment.

## 1. Think Before Coding

**Don't assume. Don't hide confusion. Surface tradeoffs.**

Before implementing:

* State your assumptions explicitly. If uncertain, ask.
* If multiple interpretations exist, present them — don't pick silently.
* If a simpler approach exists, say so. Push back when warranted.
* If something is unclear (e.g., `.proto` contract changes, transaction boundaries, or domain invariants), stop. Name what's confusing. Ask.

## 2. Simplicity First

**Minimum code that solves the problem. Nothing speculative.**

* No features or RPC endpoints beyond what was asked.
* No abstractions or Strategy interfaces for single-use code (apply OCP when variation actually exists or is requested).
* No "flexibility" or "configurability" that wasn't requested.
* No defensive `try-catch` blocks or error handling for impossible scenarios.
* If you write 200 lines and it could be 50, rewrite it.

Ask yourself: "Would a senior engineer say this is overcomplicated?" If yes, simplify.

## 3. Surgical Changes

**Touch only what you must. Clean up only your own mess.**

When editing existing code:

* Don't "improve" adjacent code, comments, or formatting.
* Don't refactor things that aren't broken.
* Match existing style, even if you'd do it differently.
* If you notice unrelated dead code, mention it — don't delete it.

When your changes create orphans:

* Remove imports, variables, fields, or private methods that YOUR changes made unused.
* Don't remove pre-existing dead code unless asked.

The test: Every changed line should trace directly to the user's request.

## 4. Goal-Driven Execution

**Define success criteria. Loop until verified.**

Transform tasks into verifiable goals:

* "Add validation" → "Write tests for invalid inputs, then make them pass"
* "Fix the bug" → "Write a test that reproduces it, then make it pass"
* "Refactor X" → "Ensure unit and gRPC integration tests pass before and after"

For multi-step tasks, state a brief plan:
[Step] → verify: [check]
[Step] → verify: [check]

Strong success criteria let you loop independently. Weak criteria ("make it work") require constant clarification.

## 5. Tech Stack & Conventions

* **Language:** Java 21+ (Prefer `record` for immutable domain DTOs/commands, pattern matching, and modern standard library features).
* **Framework:** Spring Boot 3.4+ with **Spring gRPC** (`org.springframework.grpc:spring-grpc-spring-boot-starter`).
* **Serialization / RPC:** Protocol Buffers (`proto3`) & gRPC.
* **Build Tool:** Maven or Gradle (Respect existing project configuration and `protobuf` compiler plugins).
* **Dependency Injection:** **ALWAYS** use Constructor Injection. Field injection (`@Autowired` on fields) is strictly forbidden.
* **Null Safety:** Avoid returning `null` from methods. Use `Optional<T>` for repository/service lookups that may not yield a result, and use `@NonNull` / `@Nullable` annotations where appropriate.

## 6. Build, Protobuf & Test Commands

Use these standard commands to compile Protobuf definitions and verify changes:

* **Maven:**
  * Compile Protobuf stubs: `./mvnw protobuf:compile protobuf:compile-custom`
  * Run unit & integration tests: `./mvnw test`
  * Run a single test class: `./mvnw test -Dtest=ClassName`
* **Gradle:**
  * Compile Protobuf stubs: `./gradlew generateProto`
  * Run unit & integration tests: `./gradlew test`
  * Run a single test class: `./gradlew test --tests "*ClassName"`

## 7. SOLID Principles in Spring Boot & gRPC

### S — Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)

*A class should have one, and only one, reason to change.*

* **gRPC Adapters (`*ImplBase` subclasses) & Controllers:** Responsible *only* for handling transport concerns—unwrapping and validating incoming Protobuf messages (or HTTP requests), delegating to an application service/use case, mapping the domain result back to a Protobuf response, and completing the `StreamObserver` (`onNext()` / `onCompleted()`). Never put business logic or direct repository calls in a gRPC service implementation.
* **Services (`@Service`):** Contain pure business logic and transaction boundaries (`@Transactional`). Break down large "God Services" into smaller, cohesive, domain-focused services or use cases.
* **Repositories (`@Repository`):** Responsible *only* for data persistence and retrieval. Do not include business rules in custom queries or repository implementations.
* **Mappers:** Use dedicated mapper classes or MapStruct to convert between Protobuf messages, Domain models, and JPA Entities. Do not bloat entities, stubs, or services with mapping logic.

### O — Open/Closed Principle (OCP)

*Software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification.*

* **Strategy Pattern with Spring DI:** When multiple implementations or business rule variants exist (e.g., payment processing, notification channels, discount calculations), avoid large `if-else` or `switch` statements. Define a common interface and inject a `List<StrategyInterface>` or `Map<String, StrategyInterface>` via Spring's dependency injection to resolve implementations dynamically.
* **gRPC Interceptors (`ServerInterceptor`):** Handle cross-cutting transport concerns (authentication, logging, distributed tracing, and global exception-to-`io.grpc.Status` translation) via Spring-managed `ServerInterceptor` beans rather than repetitive `try-catch` blocks inside RPC methods.
* **Domain Events:** Use Spring's `ApplicationEventPublisher` and `@EventListener` (or `@TransactionalEventListener`) to decouple side effects (e.g., sending an email after user registration) from core business flows.

### L — Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)

*Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering the correctness of the program.*

* **Contract Adherence:** Implementations of an interface must honor the expected behavior, preconditions, and postconditions of the interface.
* **No Unsupported Operations:** Never implement an interface method by throwing `UnsupportedOperationException`. If a class cannot fulfill the entire interface contract, the interface is too broad (see ISP).
* **Exception Consistency:** Subclasses or interface implementations should not throw unexpected checked or runtime exceptions that violate the caller's expectations of the base type.

### I — Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)

*Clients should not be forced to depend upon interfaces that they do not use.*

* **Focused `.proto` Contracts:** Keep gRPC service definitions granular and domain-aligned (e.g., `UserQueryService`, `UserCommandService`) rather than monolithic `.proto` files with dozens of unrelated RPCs.
* **Role-Specific Java Interfaces:** Avoid bloated Java interfaces. Split them into focused interfaces based on client needs (e.g., `UserQueryUseCase`, `UserRegistrationUseCase`).
* **Repository Interfaces:** Do not blindly extend `JpaRepository` if a consumer only needs read access. Consider defining custom base repository interfaces (e.g., `ReadOnlyRepository<T, ID>`) exposing only `findById` and `findAll`.

### D — Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)

*High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions.*

* **Strict Boundary Isolation (Protobuf & JPA):** Never leak generated Protobuf classes (`*Request`, `*Response`) or JPA `@Entity` classes into the core `application` or `domain` layers. Map both Protobuf messages and JPA Entities to/from pure Java domain models (`record` or domain classes) at the outer adapter boundaries.
* **Depend on Abstractions:** Core domain/business services must depend on interfaces (ports) rather than concrete infrastructure classes (adapters) like external gRPC stubs (`*BlockingStub`), REST clients, or third-party SDKs.

## 8. gRPC & Protocol Buffers Guidelines

* **Contract-First Development:** Place all `.proto` definitions in `src/main/proto/` organized by domain and version (e.g., `src/main/proto/user/v1/user.proto`).
* **Proto Options:** Always include `option java_multiple_files = true;` and a clear `option java_package = "...";` so generated classes are clean and modular. Never manually modify generated Java stub files under `target/generated-sources/` or `build/generated/`.
* **Protobuf Defaults & Presence:** Remember that `proto3` scalar fields default to zero-values (`0`, `""`, `false`) and cannot be `null`. Use the `optional` keyword or wrapper types in `.proto` when distinguishing between unset and default values is required by business logic.
* **Error Mapping:** Throw domain-specific exceptions in the service layer (e.g., `ResourceNotFoundException`, `InvalidArgumentDomainException`) and translate them centrally into appropriate `io.grpc.Status` codes (`Status.NOT_FOUND`, `Status.INVALID_ARGUMENT`, etc.) at the gRPC interceptor/advice boundary.

## 9. Recommended Package Structure

Organize packages by **feature/domain** using Hexagonal / Clean Architecture boundaries so transport (gRPC/REST) and persistence remain completely decoupled from business logic:

```text
src/main
├── proto
│   └── feature/v1              # .proto contract definitions
└── java/com/example/project
    ├── common                  # Shared utilities, interceptors, base configs
    │   ├── grpc                # Global gRPC ServerInterceptors & Status exception mappers
    │   └── config              # Security, gRPC, and Jackson configurations
    └── feature                 # e.g., order, user, payment
        ├── adapter             # Inbound & Outbound Adapters
        │   ├── in.grpc         # gRPC *ImplBase services & Protobuf Mappers
        │   ├── in.web          # (Optional) @RestController & HTTP DTOs
        │   └── out.persistence # JPA Entities, Spring Data Repositories, Entity Mappers
        ├── application         # @Service classes, Use Case implementations, Event Listeners
        └── domain              # Pure Java Domain Models, Records, Ports (Interfaces), Domain Exceptions
```

## 10. Coding Standards & Transactions

* **Transactions:** Place `@Transactional` on application service methods that modify state. Use `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` for query-only service methods to optimize database performance.
* **Validation:** Validate incoming Protobuf requests immediately at the gRPC adapter boundary (or via `protovalidate` / custom validators) before invoking domain use cases. Enforce business invariants inside domain models.
* **Immutability:** Prefer `final` fields in all Spring beans and use Java `record` types for all internal commands, queries, domain value objects, and `@ConfigurationProperties`.

## 11. Testing Requirements

### Unit & Persistence Tests

* **Unit Tests:** Every new `@Service` and domain component must have fast, isolated unit tests using **JUnit 5** and **Mockito** (no Spring context or gRPC server loaded).
* **Persistence Tests:** Use `@DataJpaTest` and **Testcontainers** for repository integration tests requiring a real database.
* **Assertions:** Prefer **AssertJ** (`assertThat(...)`) over standard JUnit assertions for better readability.

### gRPC Integration Testing (`@AutoConfigureInProcessTransport`)

* **In-Process Transport:** Annotate gRPC integration tests with `@SpringBootTest` and `@AutoConfigureInProcessTransport` to run the Spring gRPC server in-memory without binding to a network port.
* **Channel & Stub Wiring:** Inject `GrpcChannelFactory` into tests to create channels (`channels.createChannel("local")`) and wrap them with generated `*BlockingStub` clients.
* **Full Pipeline Coverage:** Do not call `*ImplBase` methods directly in integration tests. Always invoke RPCs through a gRPC stub so Protobuf serialization, `ServerInterceptor`s, and exception-to-`io.grpc.Status` mapping are verified end-to-end.
* **Error Assertions:** Assert gRPC error responses using `assertThrows(StatusRuntimeException.class, ...)` and verify both `ex.getStatus().getCode()` and `ex.getStatus().getDescription()`.

#### Reference Test Pattern

```java
@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureInProcessTransport
class UserGrpcIntegrationTest {

    @Autowired
    private GrpcChannelFactory channels;

    @Test
    void shouldReturnUser_whenValidIdProvided() {
        var stub = UserServiceGrpc.newBlockingStub(channels.createChannel("local"));

        UserResponse response = stub.getUser(
            GetUserRequest.newBuilder().setId("123").build()
        );

        assertThat(response.getName()).isEqualTo("Alice");
    }

    @Test
    void shouldReturnNotFoundStatus_whenUserDoesNotExist() {
        var stub = UserServiceGrpc.newBlockingStub(channels.createChannel("local"));

        StatusRuntimeException ex = assertThrows(StatusRuntimeException.class, () ->
            stub.getUser(GetUserRequest.newBuilder().setId("missing").build())
        );

        assertThat(ex.getStatus().getCode()).isEqualTo(Status.Code.NOT_FOUND);
    }
}
```

## Service boundaries

- This package is a standalone Apollo Server 5 service written in strict
  TypeScript. Use Node.js 22 and npm to match Docker and GitHub Actions.
- Apollo owns the GraphQL contract, pagination input validation, and translation
  of gRPC responses and errors. Keep inventory rules and persistence in Spring Boot.
- Use Apollo Sandbox directly at `http://127.0.0.1:4000/`. The Next.js application
  has its own entry point. See [README.md](./README.md) for a sample query.

## Schema and generated types

- Put GraphQL SDL in `schema/*.gql` and resolver implementations in
  `src/resolvers/`. `src/server.ts` loads the SDL with
  `@graphql-tools/load-files` and wires the resolvers into Apollo.
- Use the generated `Resolvers` type for resolver maps. GraphQL Codegen reads the
  same SDL as Apollo. `codegen.yml` maps GraphQL `Frame` to the generated gRPC
  output type.
- Use the [backend's frames.proto](../backend/src/main/proto/frameinventory/v1/frames.proto)
  as the Protobuf source of truth. Keep 64-bit version IDs as strings across
  the gRPC and GraphQL boundary.
- Regenerate files in `src/generated/` with `npm run generate`. The build also
  copies the canonical `frames.proto` to `dist/proto/frames.proto` for the
  runtime gRPC client.

## Validate resolver inputs

- Validate the allowed ranges and combinations of GraphQL arguments at the
  resolver boundary before making an upstream call. Keep these checks aligned
  with Spring's contract and preserve omission where Spring supplies a default.
- For each validation rule, test a valid boundary and a rejected value. Check
  that invalid input returns `BAD_USER_INPUT` and leaves the gRPC stub uncalled.
- `frames(page: Int, size: Int)` calls Spring's `ListFrames` RPC and returns
  `items`, `page`, `size`, and `hasNext`. Reject negative pages and sizes
  outside `1–50` before calling gRPC. Treat omitted or null arguments as unset
  so Spring applies page `0` and size `25`.
- The remaining operations are `frame`, `frameHistory`, `createFrame`,
  `updateFrame`, and `deleteFrame`. Pass expected version IDs to gRPC as
  positive 64-bit integer strings. An update replaces writable attributes.
- Throw `GraphQLError` with an `extensions.code` from `src/consts.ts`.
  The shared mapping in `src/frame-client.ts` uses `BAD_USER_INPUT` for
  `INVALID_ARGUMENT`, `NOT_FOUND` for missing frames, `ALREADY_EXISTS` for
  reserved IDs, `CONFLICT` for gRPC `ABORTED`, `SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE` for
  `UNAVAILABLE` or `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`, and `INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR` for
  unexpected failures.

## Logging and retries

- Cockatiel 3 supports the BFF's CommonJS build and Jest setup. Read-only RPCs
  retry only `UNAVAILABLE`, at most twice with 100 ms backoff. Every attempt
  shares the same five-second gRPC deadline. Send each mutation once.
- Use the shared Pino logger in `src/logger.ts` for structured service logs.
  Use `logger.info` for service lifecycle events such as startup. Use
  `logger.debug` for request-level diagnostics such as RPC duration or retry
  attempt number. Pino defaults to `info`. Set the logger level to `debug`
  when troubleshooting locally.
- Put diagnostic values in structured fields. Keep request payloads,
  credentials, and frame IDs out of logs. Log upstream status codes for service
  failures and keep client error messages generic for unexpected failures.
- Inspect Compose logs with `docker compose logs bff` from the repository root.

## Run and verify

- From the repository root, start the Compose service with
  `docker compose up --build bff`. The multi-stage image builds the code and
  packages its output, SDL, and production dependencies for the runtime stage.
- For a local run, start Spring, then run `npm ci`, `npm run build`, and
  `npm start` from `src/bff`. Set `FRAME_GRPC_ENDPOINT` as `host:port` when
  overriding the default of `localhost:9090` locally or `backend:9090` in
  Compose. The client also accepts the older `FRAME_GRPC_TARGET` as a fallback.
- From `src/bff`, run `npm run format:check`, `npm run lint`, and `npm test`.
  Use `npm run format` to apply Prettier. The
  [BFF workflow](../../.github/workflows/bff-checks.yml) runs the checks on pull
  requests and pushes to `main`.
- Write query tests in TypeScript under `test/`. Use Apollo's
  `executeOperation` with a stub gRPC client to check GraphQL data, error codes,
  and which calls reach Spring. `npm test` generates types, type-checks the
  tests, and runs them through ts-jest.
# AGENTS.md

Behavioral guidelines to reduce common LLM coding mistakes. Merge with project-specific instructions as needed.

Tradeoff: These guidelines bias toward caution over speed. For trivial tasks, use judgment.

1. Think Before Coding

Don't assume. Don't hide confusion. Surface tradeoffs.

Before implementing:

State your assumptions explicitly. If uncertain, ask.

If multiple interpretations exist, present them - don't pick silently.

If a simpler approach exists, say so. Push back when warranted.

If something is unclear, stop. Name what's confusing. Ask.

2. Environment & Runtime

Ensure toolchain consistency before execution.

Always check for the presence of a .nvmrc file in the root directory.

Before installing dependencies, running scripts, or building the project, ensure the correct Node.js version is active in the current shell session:

export NVM_DIR="$HOME/.nvm"
[ -s "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh" ] && \. "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh"
nvm use


If nvm is not installed in the subshell, verify node -v matches .nvmrc before proceeding. If nvm use fails due to a missing local version, stop and log that nvm install is required.

3. Simplicity First

Minimum code that solves the problem. Nothing speculative.

No features beyond what was asked.

No abstractions for single-use code.

No "flexibility" or "configurability" that wasn't requested.

No error handling for impossible scenarios.

If you write 200 lines and it could be 50, rewrite it.

Ask yourself: "Would a senior engineer say this is overcomplicated?" If yes, simplify.

4. Surgical Changes

Touch only what you must. Clean up only your own mess.

When editing existing code:

Don't "improve" adjacent code, comments, or formatting.

Don't refactor things that aren't broken.

Match existing style, even if you'd do it differently.

If you notice unrelated dead code, mention it - don't delete it.

When your changes create orphans:

Remove imports/variables/functions that YOUR changes made unused.

Don't remove pre-existing dead code unless asked.

The test: Every changed line should trace directly to the user's request.

5. Goal-Driven Execution

Define success criteria. Loop until verified.

Transform tasks into verifiable goals:

"Add validation" → "Write tests for invalid inputs, then make them pass"

"Fix the bug" → "Write a test that reproduces it, then make it pass"

"Refactor X" → "Ensure tests pass before and after"

For multi-step tasks, state a brief plan:
[Step] → verify: [check]

[Step] → verify: [check]

Strong success criteria let you loop independently. Weak criteria ("make it work") require constant clarification.

6. TypeScript Style Guide

Strict typing and modern TypeScript conventions.

Strict Typing: Adhere to strict: true compiler rules. Explicitly type all variables, parameters, and return types where inference isn't structural or explicitly clear.

Functions & Methods: All exported functions, component props, and helper functions must include explicit parameter types and a return type annotation. Inline array callbacks (e.g., .map(), .filter()) may rely on contextual inference.

Modern Syntax: Prefer modern ESNext and TypeScript features. Use standard utility types like Record<string, unknown>, and union types like string | null or string | undefined.

Specificity: Avoid using any. If a type is genuinely dynamic or unknown, use unknown and narrow it downstream using type guards or conditional blocks. Use is predicates for custom type guards.

Interfaces vs. Types: Use interface for structural object definitions that benefit from declaration merging or extensions, and type for aliases, unions, intersections, or primitives.

7. Next.js & React Conventions

Routing: Follow the repository's existing routing structure (App Router vs. Pages Router—see docs/architecture.md). Do not mix router paradigms.

Server vs. Client Boundaries: When using App Router, default to React Server Components (RSC). Add 'use client' only when React hooks, browser APIs, or interactive event handlers are required, keeping client boundaries as close to leaf components as possible. Never import server-only modules or secrets into client components.

Data Fetching & State: Follow the project's established Apollo data-fetching and caching patterns rather than introducing ad-hoc fetch calls or new state management libraries.

Navigation & Media: Prefer next/link (<Link>) for internal navigation and next/image (<Image>) for images unless existing patterns dictate otherwise.

Environment Variables: Never expose server-only secrets or private API keys with the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix.

8. Commands & Verification

Check package.json for exact script names and use the repository's lockfile package manager (npm, pnpm, or yarn):

Typecheck: npm run typecheck (or npx tsc --noEmit)

Lint: npm run lint

Unit Tests (Jest): npm test -- <path-to-test>

E2E Tests (Cypress): npm run cypress:run

9. Testing

Unit test with Jest. Cover new features with e2e where feasible.

Write unit tests with Jest for new logic, components, and bug fixes.

Where a feature involves a user-facing flow, add or extend a Cypress e2e test (see cypress/) if feasible within the scope of the task.

Don't retrofit tests onto unrelated existing code - follow Section 4 (Surgical Changes).

Final job summaries and the frame-version reference are durable. Row
diagnostics expire seven days after job completion and are purged by hourly
maintenance while the import profile is running. Worker counts and row errors
are populated by the staging and apply tasks.

### Local SQS dispatch

With the `local-import` profile enabled, set
`INVENTORY_IMPORT_DISPATCH_ENABLED=true` to poll the source queue and its
dead-letter queue. Start the `aws` and `temporal` services from the Compose import
profile.

| Variable | Local value |
| --- | --- |
| `INVENTORY_IMPORT_DISPATCH_AWS_ENDPOINT` | `http://127.0.0.1:4566` |
| `INVENTORY_IMPORT_DISPATCH_QUEUE_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:4566/000000000000/inventory-import` |
| `INVENTORY_IMPORT_DISPATCH_DLQ_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:4566/000000000000/inventory-import-dlq` |
| `INVENTORY_IMPORT_DISPATCH_TEMPORAL_TARGET` | `127.0.0.1:7233` (default) |
| `INVENTORY_IMPORT_DISPATCH_TEMPORAL_NAMESPACE` | `default` (default) |
| `INVENTORY_IMPORT_DISPATCH_TASK_QUEUE` | `inventory-import` (default) |

Dispatch verifies the exact object version and the 10 MiB processing cap, then
persists the binding before starting `CsvImportWorkflow` with the job ID as
its sole argument. The workflow ID is `csv-import-{jobId}`. Temporal reuses a
running execution and rejects a duplicate after it has closed. PostgreSQL records
confirmed starts so a late duplicate is harmless after Temporal history expires.
The workflow
execution timeout is one hour. The worker must claim the bound PENDING job
before applying inventory, and must exit if the claim fails.

Each SQS message is acknowledged after all applicable records are handled.
Failed source messages retry with a visibility delay starting at five seconds
and capped at one minute. SQS redrives after five receives. The dead-letter
consumer preserves jobs with a known Temporal execution. If Temporal confirms
there is no execution, it waits until the dispatch deadline before failing a
bound PENDING job. A valid event whose object binding never committed can fail
an AWAITING_UPLOAD job directly. An indeterminate lookup retries without
changing job state. Expired or terminal jobs and notifications for another
version cannot restart an import.

### Run the DELTA worker

Enable `INVENTORY_IMPORT_WORKER_ENABLED=true` alongside the local import and
dispatch settings. The worker reads the version pinned to the job. It restarts
staging from that object if a retry loses unlogged data. A complete staging
generation must match the durable job claim before it can be applied.

# Inventory import infrastructure

This Terraform root provisions a dedicated versioned S3 bucket, a standard SQS
queue, and a dead-letter queue in one region. S3 sends PUT notifications for
`uploads/*/inventory_frame.csv` directly to the source queue. Attach the
output application policy to the backend's existing execution role. The
backend will use the bucket name and both queue URLs as import configuration.

## Local development

From the repository root:

```sh
docker compose --profile import up -d --wait aws temporal
```

The profile pins the LocalStack community image from before token activation
became mandatory. It exposes S3/SQS on `127.0.0.1:4566` and Temporal on
`127.0.0.1:7233` with UI on port 8233. Containers on the Compose network can
reach `aws:4566` and `temporal:7233`. Use the loopback S3 endpoint
with path-style addressing when signing URLs for a host browser. The ready hook
creates the bucket, queues and notification. The smoke test is intended to run
before starting a queue consumer.

```sh
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=REDACTED AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=REDACTED uv run infra/inventory-import/smoke.py \
  --endpoint http://127.0.0.1:4566 --region us-east-1 \
  --bucket frame-inventory-import-local --origin http://localhost:3000 \
  --queue-url http://127.0.0.1:4566/000000000000/inventory-import \
  --dlq-url http://127.0.0.1:4566/000000000000/inventory-import-dlq
```

## AWS sandbox

Use a dedicated sandbox account or a dedicated stack with idle queues. Configure
a remote state backend before sharing a deployment. An existing S3 state bucket
with locking enabled (`use_lockfile = true`) and a separate key for each
environment is suitable. Store state outside the import bucket. Supply
`aws_region`, `bucket_name`, `name_prefix` and `frontend_origins` with a local
`.tfvars` file or `TF_VAR_*` environment variables.

From this directory, initialize state and review a plan with sandbox
credentials:

```sh
terraform init \
  -backend-config="bucket=$STATE_BUCKET" \
  -backend-config="key=inventory-import/sandbox.tfstate" \
  -backend-config="region=$STATE_REGION" \
  -backend-config="use_lockfile=true"
terraform validate
terraform plan -out=sandbox.tfplan
```

Apply the reviewed plan in the sandbox. AWS recommends allowing up to 15
minutes for first-time S3 versioning to propagate before writing objects.
For static validation without AWS credentials, use
`terraform init -backend=false` followed by `terraform validate`.

Run the same smoke script with sandbox credentials for the application role,
the configured region and frontend origin, and the Terraform bucket and queue
outputs. Omit `--endpoint`. It checks browser CORS headers, a signed create-only
PUT and rejected replay, version-pinned reads, version-bearing notifications,
and DLQ redrive. The script creates one unique test object and deletes only the
matched event from the DLQ. Leave the test object to the lifecycle policy.

S3 makes live upload objects eligible for expiration after seven days. On a
versioned bucket this creates a delete marker. The underlying noncurrent
version is eligible for permanent expiration after one additional day. Cleanup
is asynchronous. Keep workflow and dispatch retries within the seven-day
window. The standard queue retains messages for four days and the DLQ retains
them for up to fourteen days from the original enqueue time.

Should I integrate an existing identity provider, or build configurable OIDC support so the provider can be chosen at deployment?

I do not have an existing identity provider. Lets park this work. Authentication is a bigger topic I want to pick after this work is completed. Want to be able to do an e2e before implementing authentication

# Frontend (Next.js)

The App Router shows the paginated frame inventory, version history, and DELTA
imports. Frame history links to the durable import job summary, which remains
available after row diagnostics expire.

The browser sends GraphQL requests to the same-origin `/api/graphql` route.
Set `BFF_URL` to the BFF origin or full GraphQL URL. It defaults to
`http://127.0.0.1:4000` and Compose uses `http://bff:4000`. The existing
`/api/:path*` fallback forwards requests such as health checks to
`BACKEND_URL` (default `http://localhost:8080`).

## Local development

Run `npm ci` and `npm run dev` from `src/frontend`. For local imports, run
Spring Boot and the BFF on the host and enable their local import settings.
Start the frontend with `npm run dev -- --hostname 127.0.0.1` for this flow.
See the [backend README](../backend/README.md) and [BFF README](../bff/README.md).
In **Imports**, enter the local operator token and select the CSV file.
The browser sends the file directly to the S3 URL with the signed headers.
Keep the frontend origin in the upload bucket's CORS configuration.

The frontend keeps the operator token in memory for this session. To reopen an
import, use its job ID or select the import link in a frame's version history.
Run `npm run lint` and `npm run build` to verify the frontend.
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Suggested infrastructure for the Frame Inventory exercise.
#
# This compose file is a starting point, not a requirement. You are free to
# swap any of these services for tooling you prefer (a different database,
# search engine, message broker, hosting model, etc.) as long as the final
# stack still runs end-to-end with a single command.
#
# If you do choose to use the services provided here, pick ONE of the two
# datastores for your domain data — either `mongodb` or `postgres`,
# not both. Remove the service you do not need (and its volume) so the
# stack reflects the design you actually built.
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

services:
  backend:
    build:
      context: ./src/backend
    container_name: frame-inventory-backend
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
      - "9090:9090"
    environment:
      SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: docker
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/frames
      SPRING_FLYWAY_ENABLED: "true"
      MANAGEMENT_ENDPOINTS_WEB_EXPOSURE_INCLUDE: health,info,prometheus
      SENTRY_DSN: ${SENTRY_DSN:-}
      SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT: ${SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT:-local}
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

  bff:
    build:
      context: ./src
      dockerfile: bff/Dockerfile
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:4000:4000"
    environment:
      FRAME_GRPC_ENDPOINT: ${FRAME_GRPC_ENDPOINT:-backend:9090}
      OTEL_EXPORTER_PROMETHEUS_HOST: 0.0.0.0
      SENTRY_DSN: ${BFF_SENTRY_DSN:-}
      SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT: ${SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT:-local}
    depends_on:
      - backend
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

  frontend:
    build:
      context: ./src/frontend
    container_name: frame-inventory-frontend
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      BACKEND_URL: http://backend:8080
      BFF_URL: http://bff:4000
    volumes:
      - ./src/frontend/src:/app/src
      - ./src/frontend/public:/app/public
    depends_on:
      - backend
      - bff
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

  aws:
    image: localstack/localstack:4.12.0
    profiles: [import]
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:4566:4566"
    environment:
      SERVICES: s3,sqs
      AWS_DEFAULT_REGION: us-east-1
      SQS_ENDPOINT_STRATEGY: dynamic
      S3_SKIP_SIGNATURE_VALIDATION: "0"
    volumes:
      - ./infra/inventory-import/local/init-aws.sh:/etc/localstack/init/ready.d/init-aws.sh:ro
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "test", "-f", "/tmp/inventory-import-ready"]
      interval: 2s
      timeout: 2s
      retries: 30
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

  temporal:
    image: temporalio/temporal:1.5.1
    profiles: [import]
    command: ["server", "start-dev", "--ip", "0.0.0.0"]
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:7233:7233"
      - "127.0.0.1:8233:8233"
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

  postgres:
    image: postgres:18.6
    container_name: frame-inventory-postgres
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: frames
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: app
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 -U \"$$POSTGRES_USER\" -d \"$$POSTGRES_DB\""]
      interval: 2s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 15
    volumes:
      - postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

  prometheus:
    image: prom/prometheus:v3.16.0
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:9091:9090"
    volumes:
      - ./monitoring/prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml:ro
      - prometheus-data:/prometheus
    depends_on:
      - backend
      - bff
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

  otel-collector:
    image: otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:0.165.0
    command: ["--config=/etc/otelcol-contrib/config.yaml"]
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:9464:9464"
    volumes:
      - ./monitoring/otel-collector.yml:/etc/otelcol-contrib/config.yaml:ro

Set `SENTRY_DSN` to the BFF Sentry project's DSN before starting the service.
For Compose, set `BFF_SENTRY_DSN` instead. Set `SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT` to label events by
deployment environment. An unset or empty DSN leaves reporting disabled.

Apollo reports unexpected execution errors, internal server errors, and
upstream unavailability. Expected GraphQL validation and domain errors are
excluded. The SDK strips request data and breadcrumbs from reported events.

## Local inventory import

The BFF build packages both the frame and inventory import protobufs. For local
imports, run Spring Boot and the BFF on the same host. Enable Spring's
`local-import` profile and configure its S3 upload settings as described in the
[backend README](../backend/README.md). Set
`IMPORT_GRPC_ENDPOINT=127.0.0.1:9090` on the BFF. This makes the BFF listen on
IPv4 loopback and limits the import gRPC target to IPv4 loopback. With the
variable unset, the import resolvers return `SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE` and frame
operations remain available.

Send the local operator token as `Authorization: Bearer <token>` with
`createImportJob`, `importJob`, and `importRowErrors`. Only these resolvers
forward the credential to Spring, which verifies the token and checks job
ownership. Use the returned `uploadHeaders` values for the direct S3 PUT, then
poll the job and request row errors by page. Keep the credential and signed
URL out of application logs.
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

ready_file=/tmp/inventory-import-ready
rm -f "$ready_file"
bucket=frame-inventory-import-local

awslocal s3api create-bucket --bucket "$bucket"
awslocal s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket "$bucket" \
  --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled
awslocal s3api put-bucket-cors --bucket "$bucket" \
  --cors-configuration '{"CORSRules":[{"AllowedOrigins":["http://localhost:3000","http://127.0.0.1:3000"],"AllowedMethods":["PUT"],"AllowedHeaders":["Content-Type","If-None-Match"],"ExposeHeaders":["ETag","x-amz-version-id"]}]}'

dlq_url=$(awslocal sqs create-queue --queue-name inventory-import-dlq \
  --query QueueUrl --output text)
dlq_arn=$(awslocal sqs get-queue-attributes --queue-url "$dlq_url" \
  --attribute-names QueueArn --query Attributes.QueueArn --output text)
queue_url=$(awslocal sqs create-queue --queue-name inventory-import \
  --query QueueUrl --output text)
queue_arn=$(awslocal sqs get-queue-attributes --queue-url "$queue_url" \
  --attribute-names QueueArn --query Attributes.QueueArn --output text)

attributes=$(python3 - "$queue_arn" "$dlq_arn" "$bucket" <<'PY'
import json
import sys

queue, dlq, bucket = sys.argv[1:]
print(json.dumps({
    "VisibilityTimeout": "120",
    "ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds": "20",
    "RedrivePolicy": json.dumps({"deadLetterTargetArn": dlq, "maxReceiveCount": 5}),
    "Policy": json.dumps({"Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{
        "Effect": "Allow",
        "Principal": {"Service": "s3.amazonaws.com"},
        "Action": "sqs:SendMessage",
        "Resource": queue,
        "Condition": {"ArnEquals": {"aws:SourceArn": f"arn:aws:s3:::{bucket}"}},
    }]}),
}))
PY
)
awslocal sqs set-queue-attributes --queue-url "$queue_url" --attributes "$attributes"
awslocal s3api put-bucket-notification-configuration --bucket "$bucket" \
  --notification-configuration "{
    \"QueueConfigurations\": [{
      \"QueueArn\": \"$queue_arn\",

import './sentry'
import { startStandaloneServer } from '@apollo/server/standalone'
import { credentials, loadPackageDefinition } from '@grpc/grpc-js'
import { loadSync } from '@grpc/proto-loader'
import { PrometheusExporter } from '@opentelemetry/exporter-prometheus'
import { MeterProvider } from '@opentelemetry/sdk-metrics'
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto'
import { resolve } from 'node:path'
import type { ProtoGrpcType } from './generated/frames'
import { connectInventoryImport } from './inventory-import-client'
import { logger } from './logger'
import { createMetricsPlugin } from './metrics'
import { createServer } from './server'

async function main() {
  const protoPath = resolve(__dirname, 'proto/frames.proto')
  const definition = loadSync(protoPath, { longs: String, defaults: true })
  const proto = loadPackageDefinition(definition) as unknown as ProtoGrpcType
  const endpoint =
    process.env.FRAME_GRPC_ENDPOINT ??
    process.env.FRAME_GRPC_TARGET ??
    'localhost:9090'
  const importEndpoint = process.env.IMPORT_GRPC_ENDPOINT
  const imports = importEndpoint
    ? connectInventoryImport(importEndpoint)
    : undefined
  const client = new proto.frameinventory.v1.FrameManagement(
    endpoint,
    credentials.createInsecure(),
  )

  const exporter = new PrometheusExporter({
    host: process.env.OTEL_EXPORTER_PROMETHEUS_HOST ?? '127.0.0.1',
    port: 9465,
    preventServerStart: true,
  })
  const meterProvider = new MeterProvider({ readers: [exporter] })

  try {
    const server = createServer(client, imports)
    server.addPlugin(
      createMetricsPlugin(meterProvider.getMeter('frame-inventory-bff')),
    )
    server.addPlugin({
      async serverWillStart() {
        await exporter.startServer()
        return {
          async serverWillStop() {
            await meterProvider.shutdown()
          },
        }
      },
    })
    const { url } = await startStandaloneServer(server, {
      context: async ({ req, res }) => {
        const correlationId = randomUUID()
        res.setHeader('X-Correlation-Id', correlationId)
        res.setHeader('Access-Control-Expose-Headers', 'X-Correlation-Id')
        return {
          correlationId,
          importAuthorization: imports ? req.headers.authorization : undefined,
        }
      },
      listen: { port: 4000, ...(imports ? { host: '127.0.0.1' } : {}) },
    })
    logger.info({ url }, 'Frame Inventory GraphQL API available')
  } catch (error) {
    client.close()
    imports?.close()
    await meterProvider.shutdown()
    throw error
  }
}

main().catch((error: unknown) => {
  logger.error({ err: error }, 'Could not start the Frame Inventory BFF')
  process.exitCode = 1
})

---
name: diagnosing-bugs
description: Diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions. Use when the user says "diagnose"/"debug this", or reports something broken/throwing/failing/slow.
---

# Diagnosing Bugs

A discipline for hard bugs. Skip phases only when explicitly justified.

When exploring the codebase, read `CONTEXT.md` (if it exists) to get a clear mental model of the relevant modules, and check ADRs in the area you're touching.

## Phase 1 — Build a feedback loop

**This is the skill.** Everything else is mechanical. If you have a **tight** pass/fail signal for the bug — one that goes red on _this_ bug — you will find the cause; bisection, hypothesis-testing, and instrumentation all just consume it. If you don't have one, no amount of staring at code will save you.

Spend disproportionate effort here. **Be aggressive. Be creative. Refuse to give up.**

### Ways to construct one — try them in roughly this order

1. **Failing test** at whatever seam reaches the bug — unit, integration, e2e.
2. **Curl / HTTP script** against a running dev server.
3. **CLI invocation** with a fixture input, diffing stdout against a known-good snapshot.
4. **Headless browser script** (Playwright / Puppeteer) — drives the UI, asserts on DOM/console/network.
5. **Replay a captured trace.** Save a real network request / payload / event log to disk; replay it through the code path in isolation.
6. **Throwaway harness.** Spin up a minimal subset of the system (one service, mocked deps) that exercises the bug code path with a single function call.
7. **Property / fuzz loop.** If the bug is "sometimes wrong output", run 1000 random inputs and look for the failure mode.
8. **Bisection harness.** If the bug appeared between two known states (commit, dataset, version), automate "boot at state X, check, repeat" so you can `git bisect run` it.
9. **Differential loop.** Run the same input through old-version vs new-version (or two configs) and diff outputs.
10. **HITL bash script.** Last resort. If a human must click, drive _them_ with `scripts/hitl-loop.template.sh` so the loop is still structured. Captured output feeds back to you.

Build the right feedback loop, and the bug is 90% fixed.

### Tighten the loop

Treat the loop as a product. Once you have _a_ loop, **tighten** it:

- Can I make it faster? (Cache setup, skip unrelated init, narrow the test scope.)
- Can I make the signal sharper? (Assert on the specific symptom, not "didn't crash".)
- Can I make it more deterministic? (Pin time, seed RNG, isolate filesystem, freeze network.)

A 30-second flaky loop is barely better than no loop; a 2-second deterministic one is tight — a debugging superpower.

### Non-deterministic bugs

The goal is not a clean repro but a **higher reproduction rate**. Loop the trigger 100×, parallelise, add stress, narrow timing windows, inject sleeps. A 50%-flake bug is debuggable; 1% is not — keep raising the rate until it's debuggable.

### When you genuinely cannot build a loop

Stop and say so explicitly. List what you tried. Ask the user for: (a) access to whatever environment reproduces it, (b) a captured artifact (HAR file, log dump, core dump, screen recording with timestamps), or (c) permission to add temporary production instrumentation. Do **not** proceed to hypothesise without a loop.

### Completion criterion — a tight loop that goes red

Phase 1 is done when the loop is **tight** and **red-capable**: you can name **one command** — a script path, a test invocation, a curl — that you have **already run at least once** (paste the invocation and its output), and that is:

- [ ] **Red-capable** — it drives the actual bug code path and asserts the **user's exact symptom**, so it can go red on this bug and green once fixed. Not "runs without erroring" — it must be able to _catch this specific bug_.
- [ ] **Deterministic** — same verdict every run (flaky bugs: a pinned, high reproduction rate, per above).
- [ ] **Fast** — seconds, not minutes.
- [ ] **Agent-runnable** — you can run it unattended; a human in the loop only via `scripts/hitl-loop.template.sh`.

If you catch yourself reading code to build a theory before this command exists, **stop — jumping straight to a hypothesis is the exact failure this skill prevents.** No red-capable command, no Phase 2.

## Phase 2 — Reproduce + minimise

Run the loop. Watch it go red — the bug appears.

Confirm:

- [ ] The loop produces the failure mode the **user** described — not a different failure that happens to be nearby. Wrong bug = wrong fix.
- [ ] The failure is reproducible across multiple runs (or, for non-deterministic bugs, reproducible at a high enough rate to debug against).
- [ ] You have captured the exact symptom (error message, wrong output, slow timing) so later phases can verify the fix actually addresses it.

### Minimise

Once it's red, shrink the repro to the **smallest scenario that still goes red**. Cut inputs, callers, config, data, and steps **one at a time**, re-running the loop after each cut — keep only what's load-bearing for the failure.

Why bother: a minimal repro shrinks the hypothesis space in Phase 3 (fewer moving parts left to suspect) and becomes the clean regression test in Phase 5.

Done when **every remaining element is load-bearing** — removing any one of them makes the loop go green.

Do not proceed until you have reproduced **and** minimised.

## Phase 3 — Hypothesise

Generate **3–5 ranked hypotheses** before testing any of them. Single-hypothesis generation anchors on the first plausible idea.

Each hypothesis must be **falsifiable**: state the prediction it makes.

> Format: "If <X> is the cause, then <changing Y> will make the bug disappear / <changing Z> will make it worse."

If you cannot state the prediction, the hypothesis is a vibe — discard or sharpen it.

**Show the ranked list to the user before testing.** They often have domain knowledge that re-ranks instantly ("we just deployed a change to #3"), or know hypotheses they've already ruled out. Cheap checkpoint, big time saver. Don't block on it — proceed with your ranking if the user is AFK.

## Phase 4 — Instrument

Each probe must map to a specific prediction from Phase 3. **Change one variable at a time.**

Tool preference:

1. **Debugger / REPL inspection** if the env supports it. One breakpoint beats ten logs.
2. **Targeted logs** at the boundaries that distinguish hypotheses.
3. Never "log everything and grep".

**Tag every debug log** with a unique prefix, e.g. `[DEBUG-a4f2]`. Cleanup at the end becomes a single grep. Untagged logs survive; tagged logs die.

**Perf branch.** For performance regressions, logs are usually wrong. Instead: establish a baseline measurement (timing harness, `performance.now()`, profiler, query plan), then bisect. Measure first, fix second.

## Phase 5 — Fix + regression test

Write the regression test **before the fix** — but only if there is a **correct seam** for it.

A correct seam is one where the test exercises the **real bug pattern** as it occurs at the call site. If the only available seam is too shallow (single-caller test when the bug needs multiple callers, unit test that can't replicate the chain that triggered the bug), a regression test there gives false confidence.

**If no correct seam exists, that itself is the finding.** Note it. The codebase architecture is preventing the bug from being locked down. Flag this for the next phase.

If a correct seam exists:

1. Turn the minimised repro into a failing test at that seam.
2. Watch it fail.
3. Apply the fix.
4. Watch it pass.
5. Re-run the Phase 1 feedback loop against the original (un-minimised) scenario.

## Phase 6 — Cleanup + post-mortem

Required before declaring done:

- [ ] Original repro no longer reproduces (re-run the Phase 1 loop)
- [ ] Regression test passes (or absence of seam is documented)
- [ ] All `[DEBUG-...]` instrumentation removed (`grep` the prefix)
- [ ] Throwaway prototypes deleted (or moved to a clearly-marked debug location)
- [ ] The hypothesis that turned out correct is stated in the commit / PR message — so the next debugger learns

**Then ask: what would have prevented this bug?** If the answer involves architectural change (no good test seam, tangled callers, hidden coupling) hand off to the `/improve-codebase-architecture` skill with the specifics. Make the recommendation **after** the fix is in, not before — you have more information now than when you started.

## Verify a DELTA import in the browser

Set `INVENTORY_IMPORT_LOCAL_TOKEN` in the repository root's `.env` to a value
generated by `openssl rand -hex 32`. From the repository root, start the local
stack with imports enabled.

```sh
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.local-import.yml \
  --profile import up -d --build --wait
```

Use an empty local database for the counts below. Compose reuses its existing
database volume, so on a stack with inventory the first upload counts may vary.

1. Open **Imports** at <http://127.0.0.1:3000>. Enter the local operator token
   and upload [`inventory_frame.csv`](../../data/inventory_frame.csv).
   The completed job should show 1,000 applied and zero rejected.
2. Upload the same file again. The second job should show 1,000 unchanged
   and zero applied.
3. Open **Frames** and view an imported frame's version history. Its import job
   link should open the first job.
4. In a copy of the CSV, keep the header and one data row. Change that row's
   `status` to `INVALID` and upload the copy. The job should complete with one
   rejected row. **View row errors** should identify the invalid status.

fields = 'jobId status rowsRead rowsApplied rowsUnchanged rowsRejected failureCode'

def graphql(query, variables=None):
    request = Request(origin + '/api/graphql', data=json.dumps({'query': query, 'variables': variables or {}}).encode(), headers={
        'Content-Type': 'application/json', 'Authorization': 'Bearer ' + token,
    })
    with urlopen(request, timeout=15) as response:
        data = json.load(response)
    if data.get('errors'):
        raise AssertionError([(e['extensions']['code'], e['message']) for e in data['errors']])
    return data['data']

def upload(payload, expected_state, expected_counts):
    create = graphql('mutation { createImportJob(mode: DELTA) { job { jobId } uploadUrl uploadHeaders { name value } } }')['createImportJob']
    job_id = create['job']['jobId']
    url = create['uploadUrl']

    headers = {item['name']: item['value'] for item in create['uploadHeaders']}
    headers['Origin'] = origin
    try:
        with urlopen(Request(url, method='PUT', data=payload, headers=headers), timeout=10) as response:
            assert response.status == 200 and response.headers.get('x-amz-version-id')
            assert response.headers.get('Access-Control-Allow-Origin') == origin
    except OSError as error:
        raise AssertionError(f'S3 PUT failed: {type(error).__name__} {getattr(error, "code", "")}') from None

"""Temporal workflows for frame inventory."""

import asyncio
import logging
import os
import signal
from datetime import timedelta

from grpc import aio
from temporalio.client import Client
from temporalio.worker import Worker

from frameinventory.v1.import_worker_pb2_grpc import ImportWorkerStub

from .activities import ImportActivities
from .workflow import CsvImportWorkflow


async def main() -> None:
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
    stop = asyncio.Event()
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    for sig in (signal.SIGINT, signal.SIGTERM):
        loop.add_signal_handler(sig, stop.set)

    token = os.environ.get("INVENTORY_IMPORT_LOCAL_TOKEN")
    if not token:
        logging.info("Inventory import worker disabled. Set INVENTORY_IMPORT_LOCAL_TOKEN to enable it.")
        await stop.wait()
        return

    client = await Client.connect(
        os.environ.get("INVENTORY_IMPORT_DISPATCH_TEMPORAL_TARGET", "127.0.0.1:7233"),
        namespace=os.environ.get("INVENTORY_IMPORT_DISPATCH_TEMPORAL_NAMESPACE", "default"),
    )
    task_queue = os.environ.get("INVENTORY_IMPORT_DISPATCH_TASK_QUEUE", "inventory-import")
    async with aio.insecure_channel("127.0.0.1:9090") as backend:
        activities = ImportActivities(ImportWorkerStub(backend), token)
        async with Worker(
            client,
            task_queue=task_queue,
            workflows=[CsvImportWorkflow],
            activities=[activities.stage, activities.apply, activities.fail],
            graceful_shutdown_timeout=timedelta(seconds=20),
        ):
            logging.info("Inventory import worker polling %s", task_queue)
            await stop.wait()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

from datetime import timedelta

from temporalio import workflow
from temporalio.common import RetryPolicy
from temporalio.exceptions import ActivityError, ApplicationError

RETRY = RetryPolicy(maximum_attempts=3)
STAGE_TIMEOUT = timedelta(minutes=3)
DATABASE_TIMEOUT = timedelta(minutes=2)
HEARTBEAT_TIMEOUT = timedelta(seconds=30)


@workflow.defn(name="CsvImportWorkflow")
class CsvImportWorkflow:
    @workflow.run
    async def run(self, job_id: str) -> None:
        try:
            for pass_number in range(3):
                generation = await workflow.execute_activity(
                    "Stage",
                    args=[job_id, pass_number],
                    result_type=str,
                    start_to_close_timeout=STAGE_TIMEOUT,
                    heartbeat_timeout=HEARTBEAT_TIMEOUT,
                    retry_policy=RETRY,
                )
                if not generation:
                    return
                finished = await workflow.execute_activity(
                    "Apply",
                    args=[job_id, generation],
                    result_type=bool,
                    start_to_close_timeout=DATABASE_TIMEOUT,
                    retry_policy=RETRY,
                )
                if finished:
                    return
        except ActivityError as failure:
            cause = failure.cause
            code = (
                cause.type
                if isinstance(cause, ApplicationError) and cause.non_retryable
                else "IMPORT_PROCESSING_FAILED"
            )
        else:
            code = "STAGING_UNAVAILABLE"

        await workflow.execute_activity(
            "Fail",
            args=[job_id, code],
            start_to_close_timeout=DATABASE_TIMEOUT,
            retry_policy=RETRY,
        )

# Inventory workflows

The Python worker polls Temporal's `inventory-import` task queue. Spring starts
`CsvImportWorkflow` when SQS delivers the upload notification. Python sequences
`Stage`, `Apply`, and `Fail`, forwards staging progress as Temporal heartbeats,
and controls activity retries. Spring streams the pinned S3 object, validates
the CSV, and writes the job result and inventory versions in PostgreSQL.

## Run locally

The root `docker compose up -d --build --wait` command starts the worker.
Set `INVENTORY_IMPORT_LOCAL_TOKEN` in the root `.env` to enable polling.
The worker shares the Spring container's loopback interface and uses the local
token for the internal gRPC service. The Temporal UI is at
<http://127.0.0.1:8233>.

For a host-based run, start Spring on gRPC port 9090 with
[local imports and dispatch enabled](../backend/README.md#local-sqs-dispatch).
Then generate the Python stubs and start the worker from this directory with
Python 3.12 and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/). Use the same token as Spring.


---

Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved."
license: Proprietary. LICENSE.txt has complete terms
---

# XLSX creation, editing, and analysis

| Task | Approach |
|---|---|
| **Create** or **edit** with formulas/formatting | `openpyxl` — see gotchas below |
| **Bulk data** in or out | `pandas` (`read_excel`, `to_excel`) |
| **Quick look** at a sheet | `markitdown file.xlsx` — `## SheetName` per sheet; reads `.xlsm` too. No cell coordinates, so don't plan edits from it |
| **Read** a model (formulas *and* values) | two `load_workbook` passes — see gotchas |

> `openpyxl`, `pandas`, and `markitdown` are preinstalled — do not run `pip install` first; write the script and import directly. Only if an import fails (or the `markitdown` command is missing): `pip install` the missing package.

> Script paths below are relative to this skill's directory.

## Requirements for every output

- **Professional font** (Arial, Times New Roman) throughout, unless the user says otherwise.
- **Zero formula errors.** Never ship while `recalc.py` reports `errors_found`. If you think an error predates you, prove it: load the *original* with `data_only=True` and look at that cell. An error you introduced looks exactly like one you inherited.
- **Use formulas, never hardcoded results.** Write `sheet['B10'] = '=SUM(B2:B9)'`, not the Python-computed total. The sheet must recalculate when its inputs change.
- **Follow the user's spec literally.** Exact tab names, exact column headers, and the formula they spelled out. A redesign that computes something else fails, however elegant.
- **Document every assumption and hardcoded number** where the reader will see it — a cell comment, or an adjacent cell at a table's end. Cite a real source when one exists (`Source: Company 10-K, FY2024, Page 45, Revenue Note, [SEC EDGAR URL]`); when the number came from the user, say so plainly.
- **A workbook *you create* for someone to fill in** needs a short legend naming which cells to edit, and one example row of realistic values showing the expected format. Never add such a row to a file you were asked to edit.
- **Editing an existing file: match its conventions exactly.** They override every guideline here. Find its designated input cells first — a distinct font color, fill, or shading marks them — write only there, and leave every existing formula untouched.

## Recalculate (mandatory whenever the file contains formulas)

openpyxl writes formulas as strings with **no cached values**. Until you recalculate, every
formula cell reads back as `None` to anything reading cached values — `pandas`,
`load_workbook(data_only=True)`, and most previewers.

```bash
python scripts/recalc.py output.xlsx [timeout_seconds]   # default 30
```

LibreOffice computes every formula, the file is **rewritten in place**, and you get JSON:
`status` (`success` | `errors_found`), `total_formulas`, `total_errors`, and an
`error_summary` naming up to 100 cells per error type (`locations_truncated` says how many it
withheld — trust `total_errors`, not the length of the list). Fix what it names and run it
again. **JSON with an `error` key instead of a `status` means nothing was recalculated**, and
only that case exits non-zero — `errors_found` exits 0, so never treat a clean exit as a clean
workbook.

**A green recalc proves your formulas *evaluate*, not that they are *right*.** An off-by-one
range or a reference to the wrong row yields a clean, error-free file with wrong numbers.
Write 2–3 formulas first and check they pull the values you expect, before building out a grid.

**A workbook that links to another file loses those links** if you re-save it with openpyxl and
then recalculate. Such a formula reads `='[1]Returns Analysis'!$B$2` — the `[1]` is an index
into the workbook's external-reference list, naming a *separate file on disk*, not a sheet.
That file is rarely present here, so the cell's cached value is the only thing holding its
data. openpyxl strips that value on save; LibreOffice then has to resolve the reference for
real, fails, writes `#NAME?`, and deletes every link. `recalc.py` refuses to run in that state
— copy those cells' values out of the original before you save over them (`--force` overrides,
and accepts the loss).

## Choosing formulas that survive verification

LibreOffice implements fewer functions than Excel, and one it cannot evaluate becomes a
literal `#NAME?` baked into the file you deliver.

- **Prefer Excel-2007-era functions** — `SUMIFS`, `INDEX`, `MATCH`, `IFERROR`, `SUMPRODUCT` — which need no prefix.
- **Six post-2007 functions work, but only with an `_xlfn.` prefix**, because openpyxl writes your formula into the XML verbatim and Excel stores post-2007 names prefixed (its UI hides the prefix): `_xlfn.TEXTJOIN`, `_xlfn.CONCAT`, `_xlfn.IFS`, `_xlfn.SWITCH`, `_xlfn.MAXIFS`, `_xlfn.MINIFS`. Written bare, each yields `#NAME?`.
- **Never use `XLOOKUP`, `XMATCH`, `SORT`, `FILTER`, `UNIQUE`, or `SEQUENCE`.** The runtime's LibreOffice cannot evaluate them under *any* prefix. Newer builds do evaluate them, but they are spilling array functions and an openpyxl-written file has no spill metadata, so only the top-left cell of the range gets a value — and `recalc.py` reports `total_errors: 0` on the truncated result. Use `INDEX`/`MATCH` for lookups, and sort, filter, and de-duplicate in Python before writing the cells.
- A formula LibreOffice could not parse is written back **lowercased** — a quick tell beside a `#NAME?`.

## openpyxl gotchas

- **Reading a model takes two loads.** `data_only=True` yields cached values with the formulas gone; the default yields formula strings with no values. One pass cannot give you both.
- **`data_only=True` is destructive if you save.** That workbook has no formulas left, so saving replaces every one with a literal — permanently.
- **`data_only=True` on a file openpyxl just wrote returns `None` everywhere** — run `recalc.py` first. (A formula whose result is `""` also reads back as `None`.)
- **Merged cells: write the top-left anchor only.** Every other cell in the range is a `MergedCell` whose `.value` is read-only.
- **`.xlsm` loses its macros unless you pass `keep_vba=True`** to `load_workbook`.
- **A sheet name containing a space must be quoted** in a cross-sheet reference: `='Assumptions Inputs'!$B$5`. Unquoted, it evaluates to `#VALUE!`.

## Financial models

Unless the user says otherwise, or the existing file already does something else.

**Color:** blue text (`0,0,255`) for hardcoded inputs and scenario levers · black for formulas ·
green (`0,128,0`) for links to another sheet · red (`255,0,0`) for links to another file ·
yellow fill (`255,255,0`) for key assumptions and cells the user should fill in.

**Numbers:** currency `$#,##0`, with the unit named in the header (`Revenue ($mm)`) · zeros
render as `-`, including in percentages (`$#,##0;($#,##0);-`) · negatives in parentheses ·
percentages `0.0%`, **stored as fractions** (`0.15` renders `15.0%`; storing `15` renders
`1500.0%`) · valuation multiples `0.0x` · years as text (`"2024"`, never `2,024`).

**Structure:** every assumption in its own labeled cell, referenced by the formulas that use it
(`=B5*(1+$B$6)`, never `=B5*1.05`) · formulas consistent across every projection period, since a
lone edited cell mid-row is the commonest silent error · guard denominators that can be zero.

## Dependencies

`openpyxl`, `pandas`, `markitdown` (pip, preinstalled — install only if an import fails or the command is missing) · LibreOffice (`soffice`, auto-configured for sandboxed environments via `scripts/office/soffice.py`)

# DELTA import test CSVs

These files use synthetic frame IDs with the `CSV-TEST-` prefix. Upload them
from **Imports** in the local app. The counts assume the test IDs are new.

## Update sequence

Upload these files in order with **Force overwrite** off.

| File | Expected result |
| --- | --- |
| [01-baseline.csv](01-baseline.csv) | 2 applied. Upload it again immediately for 2 unchanged. |
| [02-newer-update.csv](02-newer-update.csv) | 1 applied. The history for `CSV-TEST-001` shows a new version. |
| [03-stale-update.csv](03-stale-update.csv) | 1 rejected with `STALE_RECORD`. |
| [04-timestamp-collision.csv](04-timestamp-collision.csv) | 1 rejected with `TIMESTAMP_COLLISION_CONFLICT`. |

To test forced overwrite, upload `03-stale-update.csv` again with **Force
overwrite** selected and confirmed. Expect 1 applied. Repeat with the flag
selected for 1 unchanged.

## Standalone cases

| File | Expected result |
| --- | --- |
| [duplicate-frame-ids.csv](duplicate-frame-ids.csv) | 1 applied and 2 rejected with `DUPLICATE_FRAME_ID`. |
| [mixed-valid-and-invalid.csv](mixed-valid-and-invalid.csv) | 1 applied and 5 rejected. Diagnostics identify invalid status, date, missing frame ID, column count, and invalid latitude in data rows 2–6. |
| [invalid-header.csv](invalid-header.csv) | Job fails with `INVALID_CSV_HEADER`. |
| [header-only.csv](header-only.csv) | Job completes with zero data rows and no changes. |
| [quoted-multiline.csv](quoted-multiline.csv) | 1 applied. The reordered headers and quoted address with a comma, quotes, and a line break parse as one record. |
